_notes: The order's own letters. E3: a friar is moved by the provincial, never by a bishop, so the diocese's offers (parish.json, seminary.json) do not reach him and these do not reach a priest of the diocese; engine/offers.ts reads `campaign`. Years away begin the week he says yes, since the provincial's letter is the order's own, and he comes home to a consultation, not the board. Flags: rome_track (fr_sem_rome_track), rome_alumnus / refused_rome (fr_rome_study, shared with the diocese's so the record reads the same). The faculty in Rome is the order's own and is not named (CLAUDE.md rule 13). QA round: formation letters (infirmary, cantor, jail, library, parish practicum) from the novice master and the master of students, and the priest's letters (mission, retreat, vocation work, novice assistant, lay chapter, review, hospital nights, novena, campus) from the provincial and the prior, so a friar's year has the order's own letters in it as a priest's has the diocese's. Flags: fr_vocation_promoter_served, fr_formation_experience. Round two: the Dominican letters (the Rosary preached in October and the public disputation in formation; Preacher General, promoter of the Rosary, the nuns' chaplaincy, the Lenten course, the summer institute on St. Thomas, diffinitor to the general chapter, the Holy Name Society) gate on order:OP. Titles and governance (the Preacher General proposed by the provincial chapter to the Master; general chapters every three years with elected diffinitors) are close to the order's practice and flagged for verification (CLAUDE.md rule 12). The mission, the retreat, the article, and the hospital nights are repeatable, two years apart, as such work is.

offers.title: The Regent's Short List
offers.body: {@master_of_students} keeps you after the term's talk. The regent of studies sends two men a decade to the order's faculty in Rome, he says, and the province has been thinking about who the next two are. He would like to put your name on the list now, so the provincial can plan a house around your absence. He is honest about what it means: a man who goes to Rome the year after ordination does not learn a priory or a parish, comes home credentialed and a little foreign, and is used by the province for the rest of his life in classrooms and councils rather than confessionals. The province, he adds, tends to trust such men with things.

accept.outcome: Your name goes on the list. Nothing changes in the house except that the lector who marks your papers marks them harder, and a student a year behind you begins, very slightly, to defer to you, which you do not enjoy as much as you expected.

decline.outcome: He says that is an answer, and that it is not the wrong one. The list gets another name. The house hears of it, as houses do, and the men who wanted a priory priest are glad.

offers.title: A Letter About Rome
offers.body: {@provincial} writes, which he does not often do to a friar who has not written first. The province has a place at the order's faculty in Rome this autumn for a licentiate in theology, three years, and the council has been thinking about whose name goes on it. He would like it to be yours. The province pays; you would live in the order's house in Rome with friars from forty provinces, sit examinations in Italian, and come home with a degree the province will use for the rest of your life, in the studium and on its councils. He is honest about the other side. The house will be a man short, and the men who have learned to rely on you will learn to rely on someone else. Some in the province will call it a reward. Some will use a different word.

accept.outcome: The house is told at chapter. Somebody says it is about time the province sent a man who could use it, and somebody else says nothing in the way that is also a sentence. Then the plane, and a house in a city that does not know you, where the Office is sung in four accents.

commitment.label: Licentiate in Rome
commitment.completeOutcome: The licence is defended in a room with three friars of three provinces on the panel, one of whom disagrees with your reading of the Prima Pars and says so for forty minutes and then votes for you. The provincial's letter about where you will be used is waiting when you land.

decline.outcome: He writes back that he understands, in a paragraph that suggests he does not entirely, and sends another man. The house is glad to keep you and says so at supper, and the province files the letter, as provinces do.

failure.outcome: The examinations in Italian are the wall, and the second year does not come. The provincial's letter is kind and short, and the house you come back to does not mention Rome, which is its kindness.

offers.title: The Infirmary Rota
offers.body: {@novice_master} stops you after conference. The brother who keeps the infirmary has a bad back, and the old men upstairs need someone at the door in the mornings: the pills sorted, the chairs moved to the window, the office read aloud to the two who can no longer hold a breviary. He says it is not a penance and not an honour. It is what the house needs this half of the year, and he thought of you. He adds that the old men will talk, and that most of what they say is worth hearing.

accept.outcome: You take the key to the infirmary. The first morning you get the pills wrong and the oldest man in the house corrects you without looking up from his rosary. By the end of the week he is telling you about the novitiate he entered, in a house the province sold before you were born.

commitment.label: The infirmary rota
commitment.completeOutcome: The brother with the bad back comes back to the infirmary. The oldest man in the house tells him you were adequate, which the brother tells you is the highest word the old man has used since the council.

decline.outcome: He says that is fine, and gives the rota to a novice a year behind you. You see the younger man on the stairs at seven with a tray, and you are not sure whether you are relieved.

offers.title: The Cantor's Book
offers.body: The cantor for the Hours is leaving the house for his solemn vows, and {@novice_master} needs someone to intone the psalms, set the tones, and keep the choir from dragging in Lent. He heard you in chapel, he says, which is not a compliment on your voice so much as on your nerve. It will cost you the hour before Vespers most days, spent with the book and the ordo, and it will put you in front of the whole house seven times a day, where every mistake is heard by men who have sung these psalms for fifty years.

accept.outcome: You take the book. For a month you start the Magnificat a tone too high and the old men follow you up without a word, which is worse than a word. Then one evening it is right, and nobody says anything about that either.

commitment.label: Cantor for the Hours
commitment.completeOutcome: You hand the book to the next man with a list of the psalms the house always takes too slowly. He reads it, looks at you, and says he had noticed.

decline.outcome: He nods and asks another man. The choir drags in Lent, as it always has, and you find that you notice it now in a way you did not before he asked.

offers.title: Tuesdays at the Jail
offers.body: {@master_of_students} has an arrangement with the county jail: an older priest of the house says Mass there on Tuesdays and hears what confessions there are, and a student goes with him to lead the Bible study and sit with the men who want to talk. The student who went last year has been sent on. The work is not glamorous, he says, and it will not appear in any evaluation. It will teach you more about sin and mercy than the tract on penance, and you will have the tract on penance next year anyway.

accept.outcome: The first Tuesday the guard makes you empty your pockets twice. The men in the study are polite and bored until one of them asks a question about Cain that you cannot answer, and the older priest, driving home, says that was the best study he has seen in a year.

commitment.label: Tuesdays at the county jail
commitment.completeOutcome: Your last Tuesday a man you have sat with all year shakes your hand through the gap in the table and says he hopes they make you a priest. You find out later he was moved to the state prison the next week, and nobody told him where.

decline.outcome: He says there will be other students. There are, and one of them comes back from his first Tuesday very quiet and goes to chapel before supper, which you notice, and think about more than you expected to.

offers.title: The Old Library
offers.body: The house library has a room nobody has catalogued since the province was founded: the books of three closed priories, boxed and stacked, some of them older than the country. {@master_of_students} needs a student with patience and enough Latin to tell a commentary on the Sentences from a book of sermons, a few hours a week for a term, to make a list. He says the list will outlive both of you. He also says, looking at the ceiling, that the room is cold.

accept.outcome: The room is cold. The second week you find a book of sermons for Lent with a friar's name in the margin and a note in pencil beside the sermon on patience that says only, not this year. You put it on the list with the rest.

commitment.label: Cataloguing the old library
commitment.completeOutcome: The list runs to eleven hundred entries. The provincial's secretary asks for a copy, and a professor at the studium asks to borrow a book you found, and for a week you are known in the house as the man who knows where things are.

decline.outcome: He says the room has waited a century and can wait another term. It does. The boxes stay where they are, and now and then you pass the door and think about them.

offers.title: Sundays in a Parish
offers.body: A pastor in the diocese has asked the house for a student on Sundays: to preach at the children's Mass, teach the confirmation class, and learn what a parish looks like from the sacristy. {@master_of_students} thinks you are ready, and thinks also that you have lived long enough in a house where every man has read Augustine. The pastor, he warns, is a diocesan man with strong opinions about friars, most of them earned by friars.

accept.outcome: The pastor meets you at the rectory door in a golf shirt and asks what they are teaching you over there. You tell him. He says fine, the children's Mass is at nine, keep it under eight minutes, and do not use the word Thomistic in front of the confirmation parents.

commitment.label: Sundays in a diocesan parish
commitment.completeOutcome: On your last Sunday the confirmation class gives you a card signed by all of them, and the pastor, handing it to you, says you will be all right, for a friar. From him it is warm.

decline.outcome: He tells the pastor the house cannot spare a man this year. The pastor, you hear later, said that is what the friars always say.

offers.title: A Parish Mission
offers.body: A pastor two dioceses away has written to the province for a parish mission in Lent: four nights of preaching, confessions until the line is done, a Mass for the sick on the last morning. {@provincial} forwards the letter with a note in his own hand. The man they usually send is ill. The province's name goes with whoever preaches it, he writes, and he would like it to be yours. It will cost you the better part of two weeks, a car borrowed from the house, and whatever you had planned for them.

accept.outcome: You write four sermons on the parable of the prodigal son, throw out the third, and write it again on the drive. The first night there are forty people. The last there are three hundred, and the line for confession runs past midnight.

commitment.label: Preaching a parish mission
commitment.completeOutcome: The pastor writes to the provincial afterwards. The provincial sends you a copy of the letter without comment, which from him is a comment, and the house hears about the line for confession before you have unpacked.

decline.outcome: He writes back that the pastor will be disappointed and the province will find someone. It does; the man comes home hoarse and pleased, and the pastor sends the house a check.

offers.title: The Sisters' Retreat
offers.body: An enclosed monastery of contemplative nuns has asked the province for a retreat master for their annual eight days: two conferences a day, confessions, the conventual Mass, and whatever the prioress asks for in the parlor. {@provincial} writes that these women have prayed for the province for longer than any of its houses have stood, and that the man who preaches to them should have something to say. He thinks you do. He adds that they will know within a day if you do not.

accept.outcome: You go with sixteen conferences written and give eleven of them. The prioress asks in the parlor on the third day what you actually believe about grace, as distinct from what you have been saying, and you tell her, and she says that is better, give them that.

commitment.label: Retreat master to the sisters
commitment.completeOutcome: On the last morning the prioress tells you through the grille that the community will pray for you by name every day for a year. You have been promised many things by many people. This is the one you believe.

decline.outcome: He sends another man. The nuns write afterwards to thank the province and mention, in the last line, that they had hoped for you, and that they will pray for you anyway.

offers.title: The Province's Vocation Work
offers.body: {@provincial} is short of a man to promote vocations: the campus visits, the weekend retreats for inquirers, the letters to young men who wrote once and then went quiet, the long lunches with mothers who are not sure. It is half a job laid on top of the one you have, for two years. He chose you, he writes, because the men who come to the door should meet someone who is glad to be here. He would like an answer within the month.

accept.outcome: The first inquiry weekend six young men come. Two of them spend the whole of Saturday asking about the food and one asks about nothing at all and watches everything. That one writes to you in March.

commitment.label: Vocation promoter for the province
commitment.completeOutcome: Two of the men who came to your weekends are novices now. One of them writes to say he would not have come without the lunch with his mother, which you had forgotten, and she had not.

decline.outcome: He writes that he understands. He gives it to a younger man, who fills a van with inquirers by autumn, and at chapter the province thanks him by name.

offers.title: Assistant to the Novice Master
offers.body: The novice master has asked for help. There are more novices this year than the house has seen in a decade, and he cannot hear them all, teach the constitutions, and keep the house besides. {@provincial} asks whether you would be his assistant for a year: the classes on the vows, the manual work, the walks in the afternoon with the young men who are finding out who they are. It is the province's most delicate work, he writes, and he does not ask lightly.

accept.outcome: The first week you teach the vow of poverty to nine men who own nothing and are worried about it, and you realize halfway through the class that you are describing yourself at their age, and that it went better than you feared.

commitment.label: Assistant to the novice master
commitment.completeOutcome: Seven of the nine make their first profession. At the reception afterwards the novice master raises a glass to you in front of the provincial, which is the kind of thing that is remembered at chapters.

decline.outcome: He says the novice master will manage. He does, just, and at the end of the year two of the novices leave, which happens every year, and you wonder whether it would have happened with you there.

offers.title: The Lay Chapter's Assistant
offers.body: The order's lay chapter meets in the house parlor on the second Saturday of every month: thirty men and women who have made promises to live by the order's spirit in the world, and who need a friar to give a conference, hear confessions, and settle, now and then, a quarrel about the minutes. {@prior} asks whether you will take them on. The man who had them has been moved, and they are, the prior says, very patient and very persistent.

accept.outcome: Your first Saturday you give a conference on the rosary and are corrected, kindly, by a retired schoolteacher who has been a lay member for forty years and knows the order's history better than you do. She brings you soup the next week.

commitment.label: Assistant to the lay chapter
commitment.completeOutcome: Three of the chapter's members make their final promises at the end of the year, and you receive them. The schoolteacher says afterwards that you have come along nicely.

decline.outcome: The prior gives them to a man who is already too busy. The chapter meets anyway, as it did through the years without anyone, and prays for a friar who will stay.

offers.title: An Article for the Province
offers.body: The province's review, which goes to every house and to a few libraries that have forgotten to cancel it, needs a piece for its next number. {@provincial} suggests you write on the thing you preach about most, at the length of a real argument, with the notes a real argument needs. The editor is a lector with sharp opinions. He will send it back twice, the provincial writes, and the third version will be worth reading.

accept.outcome: The editor sends it back with a note that says the second half is a different article and the better one. You write the second half. He sends it back again with the notes redone in the house style and a question you cannot answer, and you answer it.

commitment.label: Writing for the province's review
commitment.completeOutcome: It runs to nineteen pages. A friar in another province writes to disagree with page eleven, at length, and you realize you have been read.

decline.outcome: He says another number, then. The review goes out with a long piece on the order's missions in the last century, and the lector who edits it looks at you at chapter as if he had been promised something.

offers.title: The Night Calls
offers.body: The hospital across the river has lost its chaplain, and until the diocese finds another it has asked the house to cover the night calls: the anointings at three in the morning, the families in the corridor, the sacrament for the dying when there is no one else. {@prior} is dividing the month among the men who can drive. He asks whether you will take a week of nights in each month for a season. It is not work anyone does for thanks, he says, and it is the oldest work there is.

accept.outcome: The first call comes at twenty past two. A woman in her nineties, a family of eleven around her, a grandson who is angry that it took you forty minutes. You anoint her, and she dies before you leave the floor, and the grandson walks you to the car and does not say anything, and shakes your hand.

commitment.label: Night calls at the hospital
commitment.completeOutcome: The diocese finds a chaplain. The nurses on the night floor send the house a tin of cookies with a card addressed to the friars, and under it, in a different hand, your name.

decline.outcome: The prior divides your week among the others. The old men take it without complaint, and at breakfast one of them falls asleep over his coffee, and nobody mentions why.

offers.title: A Novena for a Patron
offers.body: A parish in the city keeps a novena every year before its patron's feast, and for thirty years it has asked the house for the preacher. {@prior} passes the letter across the refectory table: nine evenings, a short sermon after the prayers, a blessing with the relic on the last night, and a dinner with the pastor that the prior says is the real test. The people come for the saint. Whether they come back for the preacher, he says, is up to you.

accept.outcome: The first evening there are the regulars, sixty women and four men and a child who is there against her will. By the ninth the church is half full, and the pastor at dinner says it has not been that way since the old friar who used to do it went to the infirmary.

commitment.label: Preaching a novena
commitment.completeOutcome: On the last night an old woman kisses the relic, then your hand, and tells you her mother made the novena every year of the war. The pastor asks the prior for you by name next year.

decline.outcome: The prior sends another man. The novena goes on, as it has for thirty years, and the pastor writes afterwards that it was fine.

offers.title: The Newman Center
offers.body: The Catholic center at the state university has asked the province for a friar at the weekends: the Sunday evening Mass the students actually attend, confessions before it, and the long conversations after that run past midnight about God, sex, and graduate school. {@provincial} thinks you would be good at it, and would like you to try it for a year before anyone decides whether it is a work the province should take on for good.

accept.outcome: The Sunday evening Mass is at nine and the students arrive at nine fifteen. After it a young woman in an engineering sweatshirt asks you whether the proofs for God work, and you are there until one in the morning, and she comes back the next week with a friend.

commitment.label: Weekends at the Newman center
commitment.completeOutcome: Two of the students are received into the Church at the Easter Vigil, and one is thinking about the order. The university asks the provincial whether the friar can stay, and the provincial says he will consider it.

decline.outcome: He writes to the university that the province cannot spare a man this year. The students find the diocesan priest who comes on alternate Sundays, and some of them find the chapel on the corner of campus, and some of them find nothing.

offers.title: Preaching the Rosary
offers.body: The parishes of the city keep October as the month of the Rosary, and every year the studium sends student brothers out on Sunday afternoons to preach the mysteries: ten minutes on each, then the decade, then the next. {@master_of_students} asks whether you will take a parish this October. It is where Dominicans learned to preach for eight hundred years, he says, in front of people who would rather be at home and who pray anyway.

accept.outcome: The first Sunday you preach the Annunciation to forty people and a dozing usher. By the last, you have learned to stop talking before the people stop listening, which the master of students says is most of preaching.

commitment.label: Preaching the Rosary in October
commitment.completeOutcome: On the last Sunday an old man tells you at the door that his wife, who died in June, never missed the October Rosary, and that you would have pleased her. You carry it home like a coin.

decline.outcome: He gives the parish to a student a year behind you, who comes home every Sunday in October flushed and hoarse and happier than you have seen him.

offers.title: The Public Disputation
offers.body: Once a year the studium holds a disputation in the old manner: a student defends a question against all comers, the lectors object, the regent determines. {@master_of_students} would like you to defend this year's, on whether the existence of God can be demonstrated, before the house and whoever from the city wants to come. It is an honour, he says, and a small public humiliation, which is the Dominican way of doing honours.

accept.outcome: You prepare for six weeks. On the night, a philosophy professor from the state university objects from the second row, and you answer him, mostly, and the regent determines the question in your favour with a qualification you will be thinking about for years.

commitment.label: Preparing the public disputation
commitment.completeOutcome: The regent's determination is printed in the province's newsletter with your name in the first line. The master of students cuts it out and pins it to the students' board, which he has not done in eleven years.

decline.outcome: He gives it to another student, who is flattened by the lector of moral theology and recovers by the reception, and is spoken of afterwards with affection.

offers.title: Preacher General
offers.body: The provincial chapter has voted to propose your name to the Master of the Order for the title of Preacher General, which the order gives to friars whose preaching has served it for years. {@provincial} writes to ask whether you will accept, if it is conferred. It changes nothing in the house, he says, and gives you a voice in chapters; and it tells every pastor who reads the province's directory that this man can be trusted with a pulpit.

accept.outcome: The letter from the Master comes in the spring, in Latin, and is read at table. The old men applaud with their spoons. By summer three pastors have written asking for a mission, and one of them spells your name correctly.

decline.outcome: You write that you would rather preach than be called a preacher. {@provincial} reads it aloud at the council, you hear later, and the council laughs, and the chapter's minutes note that the brother declined with humility.

offers.title: Promoter of the Rosary
offers.body: The province needs a promoter of the Rosary: the friar who keeps the Rosary Confraternity's registers, erects it in parishes that ask, blesses beads by the thousand, and preaches the mysteries wherever he is invited. The last man held it for thirty years and has died. {@provincial} asks whether you would take it for three. The work is small and endless and, he adds, it is the oldest thing the order does for the ordinary Catholic.

accept.outcome: The registers arrive in two boxes: names in fountain pen from before the war, ballpoint from after, and a laptop the last promoter never opened. The first parish that asks to have the Confraternity erected has sixty people at the Mass, and a hundred and twenty sets of beads.

commitment.label: Promoter of the Rosary
commitment.completeOutcome: In three years the Confraternity is erected in eleven parishes. You hand the registers on with a note on which pastors will answer letters. The new promoter reads the old names out at recreation too.

decline.outcome: He gives it to an older friar who is glad of it. The registers go to his room, and at recreation he reads out the names of parishes that joined in 1911 as if they were cricket scores.

offers.title: Chaplain to the Nuns
offers.body: The monastery of the order's nuns, enclosed, twenty women who have kept the Hours since before the province had a studium, needs a chaplain: the conventual Mass each morning, confessions, a conference a week through the grille, and the long patience of being the only man most of them speak to in a month. {@provincial} writes that Dominic founded the nuns before he founded the friars, and that the friars have owed them a good chaplain ever since.

accept.outcome: The first morning you say Mass behind a grille to voices you cannot see, and the chant is better than any in the province. After, the prioress tells you through the turn that they have prayed for the preachers for eight hundred years and would now like to pray for you in particular.

commitment.label: Chaplain to the nuns of the order
commitment.completeOutcome: When you leave, the nuns give you a stole they embroidered over two winters. The prioress says through the grille that you preached to them as if they were adults, and that not every chaplain does.

decline.outcome: He sends an older friar who has done it before. The nuns send you a card at Christmas anyway, saying they pray for you, and you believe them.

offers.title: The Lenten Course
offers.body: The cathedral of the diocese has asked the province, as it does every few years, for a Dominican to preach the Lenten course: six Friday evenings, a sermon of half an hour on one theme, before a congregation that comes for the preaching and will say so if it is not good. {@provincial} forwards the request with the note that the bishop will be in his chair for at least one of them.

accept.outcome: You choose the seven last words and give up two weekends in February to writing. The first Friday there are two hundred people. The fourth, the bishop is in his chair and does not look at his watch.

commitment.label: Preaching the Lenten course at the cathedral
commitment.completeOutcome: On Good Friday the cathedral's rector asks for the texts, to print. The bishop writes a card in his own hand saying he had not heard the fourth word preached that way.

decline.outcome: Another friar preaches it, on the Beatitudes, very well. The cathedral's rector tells the province that they had hoped for you, which is a kind thing to hear too late.

offers.title: The Summer Institute on St. Thomas
offers.body: The province runs a summer institute for lay people who want to read St. Thomas properly: two weeks, a question a morning, seminars in the afternoon, and a disputation on the last day that the students take far too seriously. {@provincial} asks whether you will teach the question on the virtues this year. The lector who usually does it is on sabbatical, and the students, he warns, include two retired judges.

accept.outcome: The judges sit in the front row and object to everything, delightfully. A nurse in the back row asks the only question you cannot answer, about whether courage can be commanded, and you tell her so, and she writes to you for a year.

commitment.label: Teaching at the summer institute
commitment.completeOutcome: The disputation on the last day is on whether a Christian may lie to save a life. The judges lose. The evaluations say you should come back, and one says only: more Thomas, less PowerPoint.

decline.outcome: A younger friar takes the virtues and is eaten alive by the judges and is invited back by acclamation.

offers.title: Diffinitor to the General Chapter
offers.body: The provincial chapter has elected you its diffinitor to the order's general chapter: four weeks abroad with friars from every province of the world, debating the acts that will govern the order until the next chapter three years on. {@provincial} writes that it is a great deal of reading, a great deal of sitting, and the best education in what the order is that a friar can get without being elected to anything worse.

accept.outcome: The acts arrive in a binder the size of a missal. You read them on the plane. The first morning of the chapter you sit between a friar from Vietnam and a friar from Nigeria, and between them they have founded more houses than your province has.

commitment.label: Diffinitor at the general chapter
commitment.completeOutcome: You come home with a list of friars in thirty countries who will answer your letters, and a clearer sense than you wanted of how small the province is. At the house chapter you report for an hour, and the old men ask the right questions.

decline.outcome: The chapter elects another man, who goes, and comes back thinner and wiser, and gives the province a report that everyone reads and nobody agrees with.

offers.title: The Holy Name Men
offers.body: The parish's Holy Name Society, which the Dominicans were given charge of centuries ago and which the house has kept alive in the parish long after most parishes let theirs go, has lost its spiritual director to a transfer. Twenty men, most of them over sixty, meet on the second Sunday for Mass, breakfast, and a talk. {@prior} asks whether you will take them. They are loyal, he says, and they will tell you what they think of your talk before the eggs are cold.

accept.outcome: Your first talk is on the second commandment. A retired bus driver tells you over the eggs that you went on too long about blasphemy and not long enough about swearing, and he is right, and he becomes, in the way of these things, your friend.

commitment.label: Spiritual director of the Holy Name Society
commitment.completeOutcome: At the year's last breakfast the men give you a Holy Name pin their fathers wore. Two of them have started coming to daily Mass, and one has started coming to confession, which he says is your fault.

decline.outcome: The men meet without a friar for a season and then ask for one from the diocese, who comes, and finds them, he says, the best breakfast in the deanery.
